etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Middle French conductour, from Old French conduitor, from Latin conductor.

definitions.definition: One who conducts or leads; a guide; a director.

quote.citation: 1687, [John Dryden], “The Third Part”, in The Hind and the Panther. A Poem, in Three Parts, 2nd edition, London:  […]  Jacob Tonson […], →OCLC, page 96:
quote.text: […] Zeal, the blind conductor of the will;

definitions.definition: (music) A person who conducts an orchestra, choir or other music ensemble; a professional whose occupation is conducting.
(rail transport) A person who takes tickets on public transportation and also helps passengers.

quote.citation: 2022 April 6, “Network News: Booze ban continues as part of move to prioritise women's safety”, in RAIL, number 954, page 6:
quote.text: " […]  And one of the things that makes me feel safe is when I see the conductor."

definitions.definition: (physics) Something that can transmit electricity, heat, light, or sound.

quote.text: Falling conductors may come in contact with grounded objects or puddles of water.

quote.citation: 1997, Institution of Electrical Engineers, Fourth International Conference on Advances in Power System Control, Operation & Management, 11-13 November 1997, Institution of Electrical Engineers:
quote.text: The failure of HIF detection leads to potential hazard to human beings and potential fire. HIFS are usually caused by falling conductors coming into contact with a surface having poor conductivity.

definitions.definition: (mathematics) An ideal of a ring that measures how far it is from being integrally closed

quote.citation: 1988, F van Oystaeyen, Lieven Le Bruyn, Perspectives in ring theory:
quote.text: If c is the conductor ideal for R in R then prime ideals not containing c correspond to localizations yielding discrete valuation rings.

definitions.definition: A grooved sound or staff used for directing instruments, such as lithontriptic forceps; a director.
